+  // Confirmed empirically: ANTLR4 has a genuine, native `# Name` alt-label syntax (ADR D26) —
+  // `BackendAntlr.scala`'s `parserRule`/`altText` never reads `r.label` at all, so a labeled
+  // alternative renders as a bare, unlabeled alt even though the target format could carry the
+  // label losslessly. (`BackendTs.scala`, checked for contrast, DOES read `r.label` to prefer it
+  // over its own fallback name — so this is a real gap in `BackendAntlr` specifically, not an
+  // inherent notation mismatch; deliberately scoped to `antlr`/`bison` only, since only those two
+  // were verified here.) Real Bison/yacc has no alt-label concept at all — no `.y` syntax names
+  // one alternative of a rule — so the loss there is structural, not a missed opportunity, but
+  // still real: an author relying on the label for downstream tooling loses it either way.
+  def altLabelLoss(ir: IR, backendName: String): Vector[String] =
+    if backendName != "antlr" && backendName != "bison" then Vector.empty
+    else
+      val ntNameById = ir.grammar.nonterminals.map(n => n.id -> n.name).toMap
+      ir.grammar.rules.collect {
+        case r if r.label.isDefined =>
+          val lbl = r.label.get
+          val rule = ntNameById.getOrElse(r.lhs, s"nt${r.lhs}")
+          val why =
+            if backendName == "antlr" then
+              "ANTLR4 has native `# Name` alt-label syntax, but this backend never emits it"
+            else "Bison/yacc has no alt-label concept at all for it to go into"
+          s"rule `$rule`'s alternative is labeled `# $lbl`; $why, so the label vanishes on " +
+            "export (visitor/accessor method names and CST-node naming that depend on it are lost)"
+      }
+
+  // Confirmed empirically: ANTLR4's `.g4` syntax has no case-insensitive-terminal flag (no
+  // `@caseless`-equivalent token option — real ANTLR4 needs either the `caseInsensitive` grammar
+  // option (4.10+) or a manual `[Ss][Ee]...`-style character-class expansion, neither of which
+  // this backend does). `BackendAntlr.scala`'s `lexerRule` renders `cls.pattern` through
+  // `patternText`/`regexToAntlr` completely UNCHANGED, ignoring `IRTokenClass.caseless` (ADR D35)
+  // entirely — worse than a dropped decoration: the emitted `.g4` lexer rule matches only the
+  // EXACT case spelled in the source pattern, so it silently accepts a strictly NARROWER language
+  // than the caseless token class actually specifies (e.g. a caseless `SELECT` keyword no longer
+  // matches `select`/`Select` after export). `BackendBison.scala` never emits token patterns at
+  // all (`%token` declares only names — Bison itself has no lexer section, that's Flex's job, a
+  // separate `.l` file this exporter doesn't produce), so there is no pattern for it to get wrong
+  // there; this check is deliberately `antlr`-only.
+  def caselessLoss(ir: IR, backendName: String): Vector[String] =
+    if backendName != "antlr" then Vector.empty
+    else
+      val termById = ir.grammar.terminals.map(t => t.id -> t).toMap
+      ir.lexer match
+        case None => Vector.empty
+        case Some(lx) =>
+          lx.classes.collect {
+            case c if c.caseless =>
+              val name = termById
+                .get(c.terminal)
+                .collect { case IRTerminal.IRClass(_, n) => n }
+                .getOrElse(s"T${c.terminal}")
+              s"token class `$name` is declared `@caseless`; ANTLR4 has no case-insensitive-" +
+                "terminal syntax and this backend does no case-folding, so the exported `.g4` " +
+                "lexer rule matches only the exact case written — silently accepting a NARROWER " +
+                "language than the source grammar, not merely losing a decoration"
+          }
+
+  // Confirmed empirically (same grep as `delegateLoss`/`externalsLoss`): neither backend — nor any
+  // other first-party textual/code backend, `js` included, unlike `delegate`/`externals` which
+  // `BackendJs` was specifically extended to render (D51) — reads `IRRule.predicate` at all. A
+  // rule whose alternative only fires under a semantic guard (`{%? %}`, D-predicates) renders as a
+  // bare, unconditional alt: the guard vanishes, so the exported grammar accepts every input the
+  // ungated alternative shape allows. If the predicate existed to rule out an ambiguity or a
+  // context the bare BNF shape alone can't express, this is a real change to the accepted
+  // language, not merely a lost comment — exempted only for `ir`, which serializes the predicate
+  // marker as JSON and so loses nothing.
+  def predicateLoss(ir: IR, backendName: String): Vector[String] =
+    if backendName == "ir" then Vector.empty
+    else
+      val ntNameById = ir.grammar.nonterminals.map(n => n.id -> n.name).toMap
+      ir.grammar.rules.collect {
+        case r if r.predicate.isDefined =>
+          val rule = ntNameById.getOrElse(r.lhs, s"nt${r.lhs}")
+          s"rule `$rule`'s alternative carries a semantic predicate (`{%? %}`); the " +
+            s"'$backendName' backend never reads `IRRule.predicate`, so the guard vanishes and " +
+            "the alternative becomes unconditionally available on export — a different accepted " +
+            "language, not just a lost decoration"
+      }
+

@@ -746,9 +746,10 @@ everything target-specific is independent.
 | D47 | Sigil de-Yacc-ification: `%` → `name:`/`lang:`/`->`/`@` | **Settings-fence directives become YAML-style `key: value`: `%name X` → `name: X`, `%lang X` → `lang: X`. Token-line modifiers split by provenance: `%skip` → `-> skip` (ANTLR4's own `-> command` lexer-command syntax, borrowed verbatim — a bare `skip` names the one builtin command); `%external(pass)` → `-> <name>` (folds into the SAME arrow family: `->` followed by any identifier other than the literal word `skip` names a host post-lex pass, bare identifier, no parens); `%caseless` → `@caseless`; `%prec N` → `@prec(N)` (parens now, unlike the old two-word form). `%left`/`%right`/`%nonassoc` in `## Precedence` fences are explicitly UNCHANGED — real Bison syntax, out of scope.** | `%` is specifically a Yacc/Bison-ism that ANTLR4 doesn't share at all — ANTLR4 uses bare keyword blocks, `@`-action-blocks, `$`-references, and its own `-> command` lexer-command syntax — so keeping `%` project-wide bought no real ANTLR4 familiarity, only accidental Bison lineage. The redesign splits directives into "genuinely borrowed, matching real target syntax 1:1" (`-> skip` from ANTLR4; `%left`/`%right`/`%nonassoc` staying as real Bison syntax) versus "Gramaire's own invention, honestly marked as such" (`@caseless`, `@prec(N)`, `-> <name>` for external passes — this last one reuses the arrow container for a non-ANTLR4 concept, but was judged acceptable since Gramaire's own `.gram.md` files are never fed directly to real antlr4/bison anyway; full interop always goes through the IR/converters per D43's positioning). This avoids the "fake compatibility" trap of a sigil implying a semantic match that isn't real. |
 | D48 | Alternative delegate slot: `-> IDENT` / `-> IDENT(args...)` | **A rule alternative's trailing slot grows a sixth shape: `-> IDENT` delegates that alternative's action to a named implementation, instead of an inline `{% %}`/`{%? %}` action. `Alt` (Core AST) becomes a flat, epsilon-free six-alternative cross-product — `SymList Label Action \| SymList Label Delegate \| SymList Label \| SymList Action \| SymList Delegate \| SymList` — never a wrapper nonterminal with an empty alternative (same epsilon-free discipline as D27). A new reserved `ARROW` token (`"->"`) joins the Core's own lexis at the same level as `PLUS`/`STAR`/`LANGLE`/`RANGLE`/`COMMA`; confirmed zero collision risk empirically, since a bare `-`/`->` had no prior meaning anywhere in the notation's own vocabulary (an unquoted `-` was an "unexpected character" lex error before this). Extended in the same phase's direct follow-up with a parenthesized, comma-separated argument list — `Delegate : ARROW IDENT \| ARROW IDENT '(' ArgList ')'`, `ArgList : Arg \| ArgList ',' Arg` (left-recursive, matching the notation's own house style for comma lists, reusing the `COMMA` token already declared for macro-call `Args`), `Arg : IDENT \| TERM_LIT \| NUMBER` — enabling host commands like `-> channel(HIDDEN)`, `-> type(TOKEN_TYPE)`, or arbitrary custom ones like `-> my_custom(arg1, arg2, 42)`. A new reserved `NUMBER` token (`/[0-9]+/`) joins the lexis for the bare-number argument shape; the core `lr`-notation lexer had no numeric token class before this (not to be confused with `Tokens.scala`'s separate bespoke token-LINE parser, a different lexer). `Alt.delegate` changed from `Option[String]` to `Option[DelegateSpec]` (`case class DelegateSpec(name: String, args: Vector[String])`, `args` empty for the bare form) and `IRRule.delegate` from `Option[String]` to `Option[IRDelegate]` (mirroring exactly) — a breaking shape change to a field that had not shipped to any real-world consumer yet, so modifying rather than versioning it was judged acceptable. Each argument is carried through as its own literal source text (an identifier's name, a literal's unescaped content, or a number's digit string) — the IR never interprets it further. Mutually exclusive with an action by construction, not a runtime check (the grammar has no production combining both, so writing both is a parse error). Verified conflict-free under Canonical/LALR/IELR, including in `Gramaire.gram.md` (the full-notation meta-grammar), which already had its own `ARROW` token for `-> skip`/`-> pass` lexer-command modifiers and safely reuses it here since the two occur in disjoint rule contexts.** | Delegating an alternative's action to something named rather than inlined is the natural next step once actions exist as a slot at all (D3/D25) — a consumer application (or, in a later phase, a fenced implementation elsewhere in the same file) can supply the real implementation, without forcing every action into `{% %}` source text. Parameterization followed immediately once the bare form landed, since a real delegate target (a lexer channel, a token-type override, a custom host command) almost always needs at least one argument to be useful — deferring it would have meant re-deriving the same `Alt`/`IRRule` field-shape change a second time. Scoped narrowly this phase: only the syntax + IR field land; resolving the name (consumer-supplied lookup now, fenced-implementation lookup later) is explicitly deferred to the `## Externals` phase, which is a separate, later piece of work. Mirrors D42's predicate field precedent exactly for the IR-additive-field mechanics (encode/decode/validate/schema, goldens byte-unchanged when absent). |
 | D49 | `## Externals`: embedded fenced implementations for a `-> name` delegate | **A new OPTIONAL reserved H2, `## Externals` (ADR D29's "a nonterminal, or a reserved section" list gains a fifth member), holding one `### <name>` H3 subsection per delegate name, each with one or more real-language-tagged fences (` ```javascript `, ` ```rust `, …  — genuine host code, never a bare ` ```gramaire ` content-shape fence) providing that name's implementation body; one fence per target profile when an author embeds more than one. Canonical position: after the rule sections and the optional `## Precedence`, before the optional `## Error messages` and the always-present `## Generated tables` (`GramaireCheck.scala`'s `alwaysTail`/canonical-order check). A `-> name`/`-> name(args)` delegate (D48/D48-args) is now resolved, in order, by an embedded `### name` implementation here if present, else a consumer-supplied one at runtime (unchanged default). Purely additive: a grammar with zero `->` delegates needs no `## Externals` section, and a grammar with delegates doesn't have to define any of them here either. A `### name` with no fenced implementation inside it is a hard, located parse error (`Lr.parseWith`/`parse` themselves, not just an opt-in extractor); a `### name` defined but never referenced by any `-> name` is a warning, not an error (mirrors `unusedTokenWarnings`'s "warn on likely-unused, never hard-fail on merely unused" house style); the opposite shape — a `-> name` with no matching `### name` — is unchanged, unwarned, default behavior. `Grammar` gains `externals: Vector[GrammarExternal]` (`GrammarExternal(name, impl: Map[lang, code])`), populated the same way `Rule.doc` is (ADR D39): never by `Lr.parseWith`/`parse` themselves (so a self-hosted parse stays exactly equal to `Bootstrap.bootstrapGrammar`), only by the explicit `Lr.withExternals`/`parseWithDocs` opt-in. The IR gains a matching top-level, additive-when-non-empty `externals: Vector[IRExternal]` (`irVersion` stays 0) alongside `grammar`/`tables`/`conflicts` — document-level, not per-rule (unlike `delegate`, which lives on `IRRule`).** | The natural next step once D48/D48-args shipped the delegate *name* but deferred resolving it: an author who wants a grammar to be genuinely self-contained (no external wiring step) can now embed the implementation directly, while a consumer who'd rather supply it at runtime (a shared library of named handlers across many grammars, say) still can — the two resolution paths compose, they don't compete. Reusing `Rule.doc`'s exact opt-in-attachment shape (rather than baking `externals` into the self-hosted `lr` grammar itself) keeps this a bespoke document-structure/parsing concern layered on top of the notation, not a new core-grammar production — `Bootstrap.scala`'s actual productions, the self-host oracle, and the `Lr`-self-hosting goldens are all untouched, matching D29's "###+ is free presentational grouping" scoping (the `### name` subsections are validated by `Lr.parseWith` directly, not by the `##`-only structure gate). Mirrors D42/D48's additive-IR-field mechanics exactly (encode/decode/validate/schema, goldens byte-unchanged when absent). |
-| D50 | `gramaire lint --target <name>`: export-compat preflight | **A new CLI command, `gramaire lint --target <backend> <file>`, answering "will this grammar survive export to this backend, and if not, what specifically breaks?" — deliberately reusing the existing parse/IR-build/diagnostics pipeline (`Main.parseWithDocs` + `IR.buildIRP`, the same one `emit`/`check` already run) rather than a third, parallel compatibility model. `GramaireLint.gates(ir, backendName)` runs a small, first-version check set as `GramaireCheck.GateResult`s (mirroring `check`'s own structure/drift gate presentation, PASS/FAIL per gate with located `-` detail lines, non-zero exit on any finding — the same CI-scriptable convention `check` already uses): (1) **precedence loss** — confirmed empirically that `BackendAntlr.scala` never reads `ir.grammar.precedence` at all (ANTLR4 has no precedence-declaration syntax), while `BackendBison.scala` DOES consume it (D37/D38) — a non-empty `## Precedence` silently vanishes only on `--target antlr`; (2) **delegate loss** — confirmed empirically that NEITHER `BackendAntlr` nor `BackendBison` (nor any other first-party textual backend) reads `IRRule.delegate` (D48) at all: a `-> name` alternative renders as a bare actionless alt, the reference gone without even a comment; (3) **externals loss** — confirmed empirically that `IR.externals` (D49's embedded fenced implementations) is likewise read by no textual backend, so an author's embedded real-language code vanishes right along with the reference that names it. All three checks exempt the `ir` backend, which serializes the whole IR (delegate/externals included) as JSON and so loses nothing. Scoped deliberately narrow for a first version — three real, empirically-verified checks, not a speculative exhaustive compatibility auditor.** | The natural next step once export-lossy gaps existed silently (D38's "predicates/actions dropped on Bison import" and this phase's own delegate/externals findings) without any preflight surface to ask about them before running `emit` and discovering the loss after the fact. Reusing `runCheck`'s presentation shape (not `runEmit`'s "write files" shape, and explicitly NOT `runImport`'s bare-string-to-stderr anti-pattern — no location, no structure) keeps the CLI's diagnostic surface consistent rather than growing a fourth ad hoc reporting style. +| D50 | `gramaire lint --target <name>`: export-compat preflight | **A new CLI command, `gramaire lint --target <backend> <file>`, answering "will this grammar survive export to this backend, and if not, what specifically breaks?" — deliberately reusing the existing parse/IR-build/diagnostics pipeline (`Main.parseWithDocs` + `IR.buildIRP`, the same one `emit`/`check` already run) rather than a third, parallel compatibility model. `GramaireLint.gates(ir, backendName)` runs a small, first-version check set as `GramaireCheck.GateResult`s (mirroring `check`'s own structure/drift gate presentation, PASS/FAIL per gate with located `-` detail lines, non-zero exit on any finding — the same CI-scriptable convention `check` already uses): (1) **precedence loss** — confirmed empirically that `BackendAntlr.scala` never reads `ir.grammar.precedence` at all (ANTLR4 has no precedence-declaration syntax), while `BackendBison.scala` DOES consume it (D37/D38) — a non-empty `## Precedence` silently vanishes only on `--target antlr`; (2) **delegate loss** — confirmed empirically that NEITHER `BackendAntlr` nor `BackendBison` (nor any other first-party textual backend) reads `IRRule.delegate` (D48) at all: a `-> name` alternative renders as a bare actionless alt, the reference gone without even a comment; (3) **externals loss** — confirmed empirically that `IR.externals` (D49's embedded fenced implementations) is likewise read by no textual backend, so an author's embedded real-language code vanishes right along with the reference that names it. All three checks exempt the `ir` backend, which serializes the whole IR (delegate/externals included) as JSON and so loses nothing. Scoped deliberately narrow for a first version — three real, empirically-verified checks, not a speculative exhaustive compatibility auditor. Grown by a later follow-up phase to six checks, same shape, same restraint: (4) **alt-label loss** (`altLabelLoss`) — confirmed empirically that `BackendAntlr` never reads `IRRule.label` (D26) even though ANTLR4 has a genuine native `# Name` alt-label syntax it could target (checked for contrast: `BackendTs` DOES read `r.label` to prefer it over its own fallback name, so this is a real, backend-specific gap, not an inherent notation mismatch), while Bison/yacc has no alt-label concept at all — scoped to `antlr`/`bison` only, the two backends actually verified; (5) **predicate loss** (`predicateLoss`) — confirmed empirically that no first-party backend, `js` included (unlike delegate/externals, `IRRule.predicate`/D-predicates was never given a D51-style rendering), reads `IRRule.predicate` at all: a `{%? %}`-gated alternative exports as an unconditional bare alt, silently widening the accepted language rather than merely losing a decoration — exempt only `ir`. (6) **caseless loss** (`caselessLoss`, `antlr`-only) — see D53, a distinct enough class of finding (silently WRONG output, not just silently lossy output) to warrant its own row.** | The natural next step once export-lossy gaps existed silently (D38's "predicates/actions dropped on Bison import" and this phase's own delegate/externals findings) without any preflight surface to ask about them before running `emit` and discovering the loss after the fact. Reusing `runCheck`'s presentation shape (not `runEmit`'s "write files" shape, and explicitly NOT `runImport`'s bare-string-to-stderr anti-pattern — no location, no structure) keeps the CLI's diagnostic surface consistent rather than growing a fourth ad hoc reporting style. Rejected: re-deriving compatibility rules from each backend's own notation docs speculatively — every check shipped here was verified against the actual `BackendAntlr`/`BackendBison` source first (grepping for `precedence`/`delegate`/`externals` references) rather than assumed from what ANTLR4/Bison syntax is known to lack in the abstract. |
 | D51 | `BackendJs` renders `-> name` delegates and `## Externals` implementations | **The first backend to actually render `IRRule.delegate` (D48)/`IR.externals` (D49) instead of silently dropping them (D50's own `delegateLoss`/`externalsLoss` findings). A rule alt's action slot is one function value in `tablesBlock`'s `actions[]` array either way (`jsAction` for an inline `{% %}`, now `delegateAction` for a `-> name`), so `fold` keeps calling it exactly the same way (`action(tuple(kids, fields[node.rule]))`) — no second calling convention. Resolution order mirrors `## Externals`'s own doc (`Lr.withExternals`): (1) an embedded `### name` fence whose language tag normalizes to `"js"` (`Lr.normalizeLang`, now `private[gramaire]` so `BackendJs` can reuse the exact fold `actionLangOf` already applies, rather than a second alias list) is spliced in verbatim as the action, since it's already written in the same `(c) => ...` shape an inline action is; (2) with no matching embedded implementation, a runtime-resolved `externals["name"]` call — a new host-registration API, `setExternals(impl)`, baked into the generated module (`let externals = {}`) alongside the existing `tuple`/`fold` runtime helpers — a legitimate, documented fallback, not a compile error: an author may ship a delegate with no embedded body and expect the consuming application to supply it. A parameterized `-> name(args...)`'s literal args (a bare-digit string renders as a real JS number, everything else — an `IDENT` or an already-unquoted `TERM_LIT` spelling, indistinguishable by the time they reach `IRDelegate.args: Vector[String]` — as a JS string literal) thread through IDENTICALLY on both paths: the resolved function (embedded or `externals[name]`) is wrapped as `(c) => (fn)(c, arg1, arg2, ...)`, so a target function written to ignore the extra args (`(c) => ...`) simply does (ordinary JS), and one written to accept them (`(c, a, b) => ...`) receives them for real — with zero args, the resolved function is used directly as the action, no wrapper needed. `BackendJs.emit`/`emitTraced` grow a second, defaulted `externals: Vector[IRExternal] = Vector.empty` parameter (source: `IR.externals`); the Lab's own live evaluator (`LabApi.evaluatorJsFor`) re-derives it from `Grammar.externals` (`IRGrammar` itself carries no such field) the same one-line way `IR.buildIRP` does, so a delegate with an embedded implementation resolves in the Lab's Evaluate tab too, not just `gramaire emit --backend js`. `GramaireLint.delegateLoss`/`externalsLoss` (D50) become backend-aware: `--target js` was already a valid, accepted `lint` target before this phase (`BackendRegistry.findBackend`, the same registry `emit --backend` uses — not a narrower antlr/bison-only allowlist, contrary to this phase's own opening assumption), so leaving the checks unconditionally firing for every non-`ir` backend would have made `lint --target js` report a false "loss" for exactly the case this phase fixes; both checks now exempt `"js"` alongside `"ir"`. No other backend changes — `antlr`/`bison`/`ts`/`ebnf`/`dot`/`atn-ts`/the Scala-PEG backends still silently drop both, unchanged.** | The obvious first real consumer for D48/D49's deferred "who resolves a `-> name` delegate" question: `BackendJs` already had the one code path (`tablesBlock`/`fold`) that bakes a rule's action into a callable function, so a delegate is "just another action" in that same shape rather than a new mechanism. Choosing the wrapping-closure calling convention (`(c) => (fn)(c, ...args)`) over threading args as a second parallel table into `fold` itself keeps `fold`'s own per-node call site — the one place action-execution semantics live, deliberately not duplicated (ADR D13) — completely unchanged; the alternative (changing `fold` to pass args conditionally per production) would have coupled the uniform namedtuple-fold runtime to a per-rule shape it has never needed before. Rendering args as JS literals by a bare-digit heuristic (rather than carrying a real `NUMBER`/`IDENT`/`TERM_LIT` tag through `IRDelegate`) accepts a narrow, named edge case — a numeric `TERM_LIT` spelling like `'123'` renders as a number, not a string — in exchange for not widening the IR shape for a distinction no other consumer needs yet. |
 | D52 | A worked delegate/externals example, actually executed — and the eager-lookup bug it caught | **`examples/calc-delegate.gram.md`: a small `calc-js`-derived calculator (`Expr`/`Term`/`Power`/`Factor`) where `+ - * /` keep ordinary inline `{% %}` actions, `^` (`Power`) delegates to an embedded, argument-free `### Pow` implementation, `round(…)` delegates to a parameterized `Round(2)` WITH an embedded `### Round` implementation (the literal `2` threading through as a real second parameter), and a bare function call (`IDENT '(' Expr ')'`) delegates to `Call` with deliberately NO embedded implementation, left for a consuming host to supply via `setExternals`. Verified genuinely end to end, not just golden-text-diffed: `BackendJsExternalsExecSuite` (JVM-only, `core/.jvm/src/test/scala/gramaire`) lexes+parses a real input string through the example's own `## Tokens`/rules into a real `Cst` (`ConformanceLexers.tokensLexerOf` + `Table.buildTablesForP` + `Parser.run`, over the SAME undesugared `Grammar` `IR.buildIRP` builds from — `IR.irGrammarOf`'s own "flattened in `Table.productions` order" comment is why one production numbering serves both), feeds the serialized `Cst.toJson` into `BackendJs.emit`'s actual output, and RUNS it in a real, standalone ECMAScript engine (`org.openjdk.nashorn:nashorn-core`, a new `core` `.jvmSettings`-only `Test` dependency — JVM-portable, no external `node`/browser needed, so it runs under plain `sbt test` including CI's `core` job, which has no Node on `PATH`). Doing this surfaced a real bug D51 shipped undetected (its own test suite, `BackendJsSuite`, only ever golden-diffed emitted text, never ran it): a bare `-> name` delegate with NO embedded implementation rendered as a literal `externals["name"]` array element — a property READ evaluated once, eagerly, at `const actions = [...]` construction time, before a host's own `setExternals(...)` call (itself exported FROM the same module) could possibly have run yet, permanently freezing `undefined` into that `actions[]` slot; `setExternals` reassigns the `externals` *binding*, which can never retroactively fix an already-read array element. Fixed by wrapping that one case in the same lazy closure shape the parameterized path already used for an unrelated reason (`(c) => (externals[name])(c)`), deferring the lookup to every real `evaluate(cst)` call — by which point `setExternals` has had its chance. `BackendJsSuite`'s matching assertion updated to check for the wrapped form (and to assert the bare, unwrapped form is now ABSENT).** | The stated point of this phase was a worked example that actually demonstrates the feature, not just parses — so it was built to the same bar this project already holds other backends to (`check-atn-ts-parity.mjs` compiles+runs emitted TypeScript; `check-scala-peg-parity.mjs` compiles+runs emitted Scala), just scoped to a single JVM-test-only dependency (`nashorn-core`) instead of a second CI job, since `BackendJs`'s output is plain, dependency-free ECMAScript with nothing else to stand up. The bug this caught is exactly the risk golden-text assertions can't see: `BackendJsSuite`'s own tests for the D51 phase all passed while shipping output that would `TypeError` on every single real invocation of an unresolved bare delegate — string-shape correctness and runtime correctness are different claims, and only the second is what a grammar author or a consuming host actually experiences. |
+| D53 | `lint`'s `caselessLoss`: a silently WRONG export, not just a silently lossy one | **`GramaireLint.caselessLoss` (`--target antlr` only) catches a qualitatively different failure mode than D50's original three checks or this same phase's own `altLabelLoss`/`predicateLoss`: those all silently DROP a decoration or a guard, but the exported `.g4` still accepts (a superset of) the same strings on the symbols it does render. A `@caseless` token class (`IRTokenClass.caseless`, D35) is different — confirmed empirically that `BackendAntlr.scala`'s `lexerRule` renders `cls.pattern` through `regexToAntlr` completely UNCHANGED, with no case-folding and no ANTLR4 `caseInsensitive` option emitted, so the generated lexer rule matches only the EXACT case spelled in the source pattern. The exported grammar therefore accepts a strictly NARROWER language than the one actually declared — e.g. a caseless `SELECT` keyword stops matching `select`/`Select` post-export — silently WRONG output a grammar author could ship and only discover when real lowercase input a caseless class was supposed to admit gets rejected, not merely a diagnostic-quality regression. `BackendBison.scala` was checked too and found genuinely N/A: Bison emits no lexer patterns at all (`%token` names only — lexis is Flex's job, a separate `.l` file this exporter never produces), so there is no rendered pattern for `caseless` to corrupt there; the check is deliberately `antlr`-only, not asymmetric by omission.** | Broken out as its own decision, per this phase's own stated rule (lean toward growing D50's row in place for "more checks in the same command," a new row only for a genuinely new *class* of finding): "accepts a different language than intended" is a strictly more dangerous failure than "loses a decoration downstream tooling wanted," since it can pass every naive glance at the emitted `.g4` (the rule text looks entirely plausible) and only fails on real input at the exact case the source grammar meant to admit — worth flagging as its own decision rather than folding silently into the same bucket as `precedenceLoss`/`delegateLoss`/`externalsLoss`/`altLabelLoss`/`predicateLoss`, all five of which are "vanishes, doesn't corrupt." |
